posts.title: Chasing Shadows: The Quest for Dark Matter Candidates
posts.excerpt: The universe is far more crowded than our eyes let on. Last month, while refining our computational models at the observatory, I realized that the silence between the stars isn't empty—it's heavy with the invisible.
posts.content:
The universe is far more crowded than our eyes let on. Last month, while refining our computational models at the observatory, I realized that the silence between the stars isn't empty—it's heavy with the invisible.

Dark matter accounts for roughly 27% of the universe's total mass-energy content, yet it has never been directly observed. We infer its existence through gravitational effects on visible matter, the large-scale structure of the universe, and the cosmic microwave background.

In our latest simulation runs, we tested five candidate particles—axions, sterile neutrinos, and three WIMP variants—against observed galaxy rotation curves. The results were sobering: none fit perfectly, but the axion model came closest, deviating by only 3.2% in the outer galactic halo.

The next phase involves cross-referencing with the latest data from the Dark Energy Survey. If the pattern holds, we may be narrowing in on the ghost that holds our universe together.

posts.title: The PhD Paradox: Balancing Simulation and Sanity
posts.excerpt: They don't tell you that half of a PhD is waiting for code to compile and the other half is questioning your own existence. Here's how I'm learning to manage both.
posts.content:
They don't tell you that half of a PhD is waiting for code to compile and the other half is questioning your own existence. Here's how I'm learning to manage both.

Week three of a broken N-body simulation. My advisor keeps asking for updates. My coffee has gone cold for the fourth time today. This is the glamorous life of an astrophysics PhD student.

The honest truth is that graduate school is a masterclass in delayed gratification. You pour weeks into a model only to discover a sign error that invalidates everything. You celebrate small wins—a plot that finally makes sense, a paper accepted after two rejections.

What keeps me grounded: a strict no-screens after 9pm rule, weekly hikes, and a reading group where we discuss anything except physics. The research will always be there. Your mental health, if neglected, may not be.

If you're in the thick of it too—you're not alone. The stars waited billions of years; your thesis can wait until tomorrow morning.

posts.title: First Light: My Journey into Radio Astronomy
posts.excerpt: Radio waves are the hidden whispers of the cosmos. In this post, I break down the fundamentals of signal processing for astronomy students.
posts.content:
Radio waves are the hidden whispers of the cosmos. In this post, I break down the fundamentals of signal processing for astronomy students.

Unlike optical telescopes that capture light your eyes can see, radio telescopes detect electromagnetic radiation in the radio frequency range—roughly 10 MHz to 100 GHz. This opens up an entirely different view of the universe: pulsars, quasars, the cosmic microwave background, and even potential biosignatures.

Getting started requires understanding three core concepts: antenna gain, noise temperature, and Fourier transforms. The signal you receive is almost always buried in noise, so your first job is always signal-to-noise ratio improvement.

I recommend starting with Python's astropy and scipy.signal libraries. Plot a raw IQ sample, apply a bandpass filter, then run an FFT. That first clean peak in the frequency domain—your first light—is a feeling you won't forget.

posts.title: Stardust and Silicon: Machine Learning in Space
posts.excerpt: AI is transforming astronomy. Discover how neural networks are helping researchers identify patterns hidden inside massive datasets.
posts.content:
AI is transforming astronomy. Discover how neural networks are helping researchers identify patterns hidden inside massive datasets.

The Square Kilometre Array will generate roughly 700 petabytes of data per year when fully operational. No human team can manually process that. Enter machine learning.

Convolutional neural networks are now routinely used for galaxy morphology classification—tasks that once took teams of volunteers months to complete can be done in hours with over 95% accuracy. Recurrent networks and transformers are being applied to time-series data from variable stars and exoplanet transits.

Our group recently adapted a Vision Transformer model to classify anomalous X-ray sources in archival Chandra data. We found 14 previously uncatalogued ultra-luminous X-ray source candidates. Three are now confirmed after follow-up observations.

The lesson: the cosmos is drowning us in data. Silicon is becoming as essential to astronomy as glass.

posts.title: Event Horizon: Imaging Black Holes with VLBI
posts.excerpt: The first image of a black hole was a triumph of global collaboration. Here's what goes into building a planet-sized telescope.
posts.content:
The first image of a black hole was a triumph of global collaboration. Here's what goes into building a planet-sized telescope.

Very Long Baseline Interferometry combines signals from radio telescopes spread across the globe, effectively creating a dish the size of Earth. The resolution achieved is equivalent to reading a newspaper in New York from a cafe in Paris.

The Event Horizon Telescope collaboration synchronized eight observatories using atomic clocks accurate to a single second over millions of years. The data—petabytes of it—was physically shipped on hard drives to correlation centers in the US and Europe.

What emerged after two years of processing was the now-iconic orange ring of M87: the shadow of a black hole 6.5 billion times the mass of our Sun, 55 million light-years away. Science has never looked so good.

posts.title: Python for Astronomers: A Practical Guide
posts.excerpt: From AstroPy to Matplotlib, here are the essential Python tools every astronomy student should have in their toolkit.
posts.content:
From AstroPy to Matplotlib, here are the essential Python tools every astronomy student should have in their toolkit.

The astronomy Python ecosystem has matured enormously in the last decade. Where researchers once wrestled with IRAF and Fortran, today a handful of well-maintained packages cover most use cases.

Start with astropy for units, coordinates, FITS file I/O, and time handling. Add numpy and scipy for numerical work. Use matplotlib for plotting and astroquery to pull data directly from Vizier, SIMBAD, or the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

For spectroscopy, specutils is invaluable. For image reduction, ccdproc handles bias subtraction, flat fielding, and cosmic ray rejection. Once you have these six libraries, you can tackle 90% of observational data reduction tasks without leaving a Jupyter notebook.

posts.title: Life at the Observatory: A Night Shift Diary
posts.excerpt: Cold coffee, red lights, and the Milky Way overhead. A candid look at what a night of observing actually feels like.
posts.content:
Cold coffee, red lights, and the Milky Way overhead. A candid look at what a night of observing actually feels like.

The alarm goes off at 10pm. Most people are winding down; I'm just starting. I pack thermals, a red-light torch, and enough snacks to survive until sunrise.

The dome takes 20 minutes to cool down to ambient temperature—open it too early and thermal turbulence ruins your seeing. While waiting, I run calibration frames: bias, darks, flats. Unglamorous but essential.

By midnight the target is at zenith. The guiding is locked. For the next four hours the telescope does its quiet, patient work while I monitor the readouts, sip lukewarm coffee, and occasionally step outside to stare up at the same sky I'm measuring. That part never gets old.

posts.title: Gravitational Waves: A New Ear on the Universe
posts.excerpt: LIGO changed everything. Understanding gravitational wave astronomy and what the next generation of detectors will reveal.
posts.content:
LIGO changed everything. Understanding gravitational wave astronomy and what the next generation of detectors will reveal.

On September 14, 2015, two black holes—29 and 36 solar masses—merged 1.3 billion light-years away. The resulting chirp, a fraction of a second long, stretched and compressed the LIGO mirrors by less than one-thousandth the diameter of a proton. We detected it anyway.

Gravitational wave astronomy is now a mature field. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network has catalogued over 90 compact binary mergers. Each event is a laboratory for testing general relativity in the strong-field regime.

The next generation—Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer—will be 10x more sensitive, detecting mergers across most of the observable universe. We are, quite literally, learning to hear the cosmos.

posts.title: The Cosmic Web: Mapping Large-Scale Structure
posts.excerpt: Filaments, voids, and galaxy clusters — the universe has a skeleton. Our team is building the most detailed map of it yet.
posts.content:
Filaments, voids, and galaxy clusters—the universe has a skeleton. Our team is building the most detailed map of it yet.

On scales larger than 100 megaparsecs, the universe stops looking random and starts looking like a sponge. Galaxies cluster along thin filaments that connect at dense nodes, surrounding vast empty voids hundreds of millions of light-years across.

Mapping this structure requires redshift surveys of millions of galaxies. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey gave us our first detailed view. DESI, currently operating at Kitt Peak, will map 40 million galaxies and quasars over five years.

Our group contributes N-body simulations that predict how dark matter halos should cluster given different cosmological parameters. Matching simulation to observation lets us constrain the values of Omega_m and sigma_8 with percent-level precision.

posts.title: Surviving Your First Conference as a PhD Student
posts.excerpt: Poster sessions, imposter syndrome, and free coffee. Here's what I wish someone had told me before my first AAS meeting.
posts.content:
Poster sessions, imposter syndrome, and free coffee. Here's what I wish someone had told me before my first AAS meeting.

I stood in front of my poster for three hours at the American Astronomical Society winter meeting, rehearsing my two-minute pitch to anyone who slowed down. Mostly people just nodded and moved on. Three people actually stopped and asked real questions. One of them became a collaborator.

Tip one: your poster doesn't need to tell everything. It needs to start a conversation. Put the key result front and center in large font. The rest is detail.

Tip two: go to talks outside your subfield. The best ideas come from unexpected collisions. I attended a talk on pulsar timing arrays expecting to be lost—I left with an idea I'm still developing.

Tip three: eat breakfast. Conference days are long. Networking on an empty stomach is a bad idea.

posts.title: Exoplanet Atmospheres: The Next Frontier
posts.excerpt: JWST is revolutionising what we can learn about planets orbiting distant stars. The hunt for biosignatures has truly begun.
posts.content:
JWST is revolutionising what we can learn about planets orbiting distant stars. The hunt for biosignatures has truly begun.

Transmission spectroscopy works by measuring the tiny dip in starlight as a planet crosses its host star. Different molecules absorb at different wavelengths, leaving fingerprints in the spectrum. With Hubble we could detect water vapour in hot Jupiter atmospheres. With JWST we can do vastly more.

Early JWST results already show CO2 in the atmosphere of WASP-39b—a first detection of this molecule in an exoplanet atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is a marker of chemical complexity. It isn't life, but it's the kind of chemistry that matters.

The real prize is a rocky planet in the habitable zone. TRAPPIST-1e is the top candidate. JWST observations are underway. The results, expected over the next two years, could be the most consequential in the history of astronomy.

posts.title: Writing Your First Research Paper: A Survival Guide
posts.excerpt: The blank LaTeX file is terrifying. Here's a step-by-step approach to turning your results into a publishable manuscript.
posts.content:
The blank LaTeX file is terrifying. Here's a step-by-step approach to turning your results into a publishable manuscript.

Start with the figures. Before writing a single word, decide which three to five plots tell your story. Every section of the paper exists to support those figures. Abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion—they all flow from the visuals.

Write the methods section first. It's the most mechanical part and building momentum matters. Then results, then discussion, then introduction, then abstract. Yes, the introduction last—you can only properly frame the question once you know the answer.

For LaTeX, use the journal's own template from day one. Reformatting at submission stage is a painful waste of time. Keep your bibliography in BibTeX and cite as you write, not after.

Expect your advisor to return the first draft covered in red. That's not failure—that's the process. The best papers are rewritten five times. Start early.
